title_en: Erin Moriarity: My Dad Lost About $1.5 Million on Bad Investments. Here’s How to Avoid His
title_zh: Erin Moriarty（Erin Talks Money）：我爸爸因糟糕投资亏了约 150 万美元，如何避开他的错误
subtitle_zh: 理财科普博主 Erin Moriarty 谈 Social Security、退休提取、长期护理与晚年顾问的真实价值。
summary_zh: 本期 The Long View 由 Christine Benz 与 Amy Arnott 对话 YouTube 频道 Erin Talks Money 创始人 Erin Moriarty。她持金融学位、修完 Ohio State University 的 CFP 课程，因军人家庭频繁搬迁难以坐班服务客户，遂在疫情期间开频道，免费服务被传统理财顾问门槛（常约一百万美元）挡在外面的美国中产。标题源自她父亲因糟糕投资亏损约 150 万美元的教训。Moriarty 主张用具体带数字的例子、并遵循尽可能简化但不失真的脚本哲学做金融教育；她用个股（如 Campbell Soup、McDonald's）勾起孩子兴趣，但强调预测股市远比想象难。她谈到退休支出常呈递减而非恒定，应兼顾偶发性支出并善用护栏法（guardrails）；澄清所谓 70% 需要长期护理被误读——真正住进护理机构者约 10%、平均停留约三年；主张 Social Security 若拖得起就晚领以抬高收入底线（income floor），反对恐惧驱动的提前领取。她还强调即便 DIY 投资者，晚年与顾问合作、防范认知衰退仍极具价值。是一堂面向普通家庭的退休规划科普课。

If they can't understand it, if they can't apply it to their life, it does no good. It's very important that information is conveyed in a way that every person could understand. I say,
turns.zh: 大意是：把一切尽可能地简化，但不要简化到失真。那是我写脚本时的指导哲学。我们尽可以用专业术语，尽可以甩一张别人未必看得懂的图表，可那帮不到他们。如果他们看不懂、没法用到自己的生活里，就毫无价值。信息必须用每个人都能理解的方式传达，这非常重要。我会说，

turns.en: break it down as simply as possible. Explain it to a 10-year-old. If you can't explain it to a 10-year-old, you don't know the concept well enough and then just remember that money carries a lot of emotion. The people who are coming into your office, the people who are watching your video trying to connect with you, they have a different money script based on how they grew up, so I really approach money from a non-judgmental way because you might have strong feelings about
turns.zh: 把它拆到最简单。讲给 10 岁小孩听。如果你没法给 10 岁小孩讲明白，说明你自己还没真正吃透这个概念。然后，请记住：钱这个东西承载了大量情绪。走进你办公室的人、看视频试图与你建立联结的人，成长背景不同，各自有不同的金钱剧本（money script），所以我真的不带评判地谈钱，因为一旦你对

turns.en: saving or spending or any and all of those categories. I think if you attach any good or bad feelings to those, you're boxing people out of wanting to work with you.
turns.zh: 储蓄、消费或其中任何一类钱的事附加了好或恶的情绪，你实际上就把一批人挡在了门外。

turns.en: I wanted to ask, obviously there is a whole lot of financial content, a lot of financial videos on YouTube and TikTok and places like that. How about for consumers of those materials, do you have any advice for them when they're trying to discern who can I trust here or who should I not trust? There's a lot of deep fakes and other things like that. How about consumers attempting to navigate this space? I would say look for people who cite resources,
turns.zh: 我想问问，现在 YouTube、TikTok 之类的地方显然有海量理财内容。作为这些内容的消费者，你有什么建议帮大家分辨——我该信任谁、不该信任谁？里面有很多深度伪造（deep fake）之类的东西。消费者该如何在这块领域里导航？我的建议是，去找那些会列出信息来源的人，

turns.en: they're citing studies and they're linking them in their description, so you can kind of fact check those or use the sniff test if something sounds too good to be true or if it sounds like it's epically awful. Usually that's not true and warns further investigation because most things are not all good or all bad. I'm kind of weary of TikTok, Instagram, shorts on YouTube because I think it's really hard to convey anything meaningful in finance
turns.zh: 他们会引用研究、在简介里附上链接，这样你可以自己做事实核查。或者用'闻一闻'的本能：如果一件事听起来好得不像真的，或者糟糕得离谱，那通常都不是真的，值得进一步调查，因为大多数事都不是全好或全坏。我对 TikTok、Instagram、YouTube 上的短视频有点戒备，因为我觉得很难在 60 秒内

turns.en: within a 60-second period. I do shorts on my channel but they are cuts from my long-form videos and I link the long-form videos there and truly I only do it because the YouTube algorithm doesn't push your long-form videos as well if you don't do shorts.
turns.zh: 把金融里任何有意义的内容讲清楚。我自己频道也做短视频，但它们都是从我的长视频里剪出来的，我会把长视频链接放上去。而且说实话，我做短视频只是因为：你不做短视频的话，YouTube 算法就不会那么卖力地推你的长视频。

turns.en: So as we've touched on a lot of your videos focus on retirement readiness and decisions related to that, are there any areas of retirement planning where you think the conventional wisdom is off base?
turns.zh: 我们聊到，你很多视频都聚焦退休准备和与之相关的决策。在退休规划这个领域，有没有哪些地方的常规共识，你觉得其实跑偏了？

turns.en: I think we kind of push general rules a little bit too much if we could speak to say the 4% rule and I love Bill Bengin. I respect his research. I think he's done so much for the financial community. He came out with the 4% rule in the 90s when people were thinking, oh, you can draw 8% from your portfolio or 9% because the stock market was just booming. So he came out with kind of this contrarian perspective looking backward at the times where the market was not
turns.zh: 我觉得我们多少有点太依赖'一刀切的规则'了。就说 4% 规则（4% rule）——我很喜欢 Bill Bengen，我敬重他的研究，他为金融界贡献了太多。他 90 年代提出 4% 规则时，正值股市一路暴涨、人们想着'哇，从组合里提 8%、9% 也行'，所以他其实是一个逆潮流的视角，回看历史上那些市场

turns.en: good. I think it's a wonderful starting point but I also think when we use these dogmatic rules, we're kind of looking at things as black and white or we're assuming people don't have the ability to adapt their behavior or change their behavior in response to the economy they're in and we all know that's not true. We know people have the ability to change their budget or that their spending habits are going to change over time. I can't assume that how I'm spending today
turns.zh: 不太平的年代。我觉得它是很好的起点。但我也觉得，当我们把这些教条化的规则用成非黑即白的东西时，我们等于在假设人们没有能力根据自己所处的经济环境去调整、改变行为——而我们知道那不是事实。我们知道人有能力改变预算，消费习惯也会随时间变化。我不能假设我 38 岁今天的开销方式

turns.en: at 38 is going to be how I'm spending at 48 or 58 or 68. So I think acknowledging that life changes, desires change, things like that. So our finances have to change. We have to be adaptable.
turns.zh: 会是我 48 岁、58 岁、68 岁的开销方式。所以我觉得，要承认生活在变、欲望在变，诸如此类。既然这样，我们的财务也得跟着变，我们必须有弹性。

turns.en: So anything that's saying this is always right, this is always wrong, this is a solid rule, I think that's what deserves pushback. Do you have a favorite sort of retirement spending policy that you like to talk to people about like don't use this fixed real withdrawal system that underpins the 4% guideline, use this other one instead? What's the spending strategy that you think makes sense? I'm going to speak in generalities because I don't think anything applies to everyone.
turns.zh: 凡是那种'这永远对、那永远错、这是铁律'的说法，我觉得都值得被顶一顶。你自己最推崇的退休支出策略是哪一种？比如说，不用 4% 准则底下那套固定实际提取（fixed real withdrawal）体系，而换另一种？你觉得讲得通的支出策略是什么？我会讲个大概，因为我不觉得任何东西适用于所有人。

turns.en: I tend to believe in the retirement spending smile. I think people are going to tend to spend more in their early retirement years. I think as you go on in retirement it will decline because when you're mid 70s or mid 80s you have a most people have a lesser desire to travel and maybe our home is paid off. So I think that's a pattern we see. I do think for some people it ticks up at the end of life due to health care expenses but not as much as it was in those early retirement
turns.zh: 我比较认同退休支出微笑曲线（retirement spending smile）。我认为人们往往在退休头几年花得更多；随着退休往后走会递减，因为到了 70 多岁中期、80 多岁中期，大多数人的旅行欲望会淡一些，也许房子也还清了贷款。所以这是我们看到的规律。我也承认，有些人生命最后阶段会因为医疗支出往上翘一下，但通常不及

turns.en: years. So I think that declining spending pattern is very common. I do think people should plan for episodic spending as well because you might have a water heater that needs to be replaced, you might have windows that need to be replaced. So assuming that fixed spending is probably just not realistic. And I think guardrails are wonderful because there are going to be some years where the market is doing great and you should give yourself permission to spend more and if the
turns.zh: 退休头几年那个高度。所以这种递减的支出模式非常常见。我也觉得人们应该为'偶发性支出'做规划，因为你可能得换个热水器，可能得换窗户。所以假设支出是恒定的，多半不现实。而且我觉得'护栏法'（guardrails）非常好用，因为总有些年份市场表现出色，那时候你要允许自己多花一点；如果

turns.en: market is down cut back a little bit and that can do wonders for making your portfolio last a longer period of time while also giving you the freedom to enjoy more of your money if you're spending more during those up years. So flexibility is kind of my big thing. So obviously we've had a pretty long running bull market in the US. We've had a few downturns like early 2020 and the full year in 2022 but they've been pretty short-lived. Do you think that the average investor is maybe
turns.zh: 市场下跌，就收紧一些。这样做既能拉长你投资组合的续航，又能让你在上行年份更自在地享受你的钱，两全其美。所以'灵活'算是我的一大主张。显然美国经历了相当长的一轮牛市，中间也有过几次下跌，比如 2020 年初、2022 全年，但都相当短暂。你觉得普通投资者是不是

turns.en: a little too optimistic about stocks' ability to generate 10% plus annualized gains kind of indefinitely? And if you do, how would you encourage people to tone down their expectations so they're more realistic? I would say it's not just the average investor. I would say it's most investors. I think we are so linked to what is happening now. We have a recency bias. So if the market is doing great now, we assume it's going to be great next year. If the market is doing
turns.zh: 对股票能无限期跑出 10% 以上年化收益这件事有点过于乐观了？如果是，你会怎么鼓励人们把预期调得更现实？我会说不只是普通投资者，我会说几乎所有投资者都这样。我们太被'当下'绑住了，我们有近因偏差（recency bias）。市场现在表现好，我们就默认明年也好；市场现在

turns.en: poorly now, we think it's going to do poorly next year. I think what really helps is looking at the data and I know a lot of times the average investor may not want to do that, but bear markets do happen. Most of them are fairly short-lived. I would say less than 24 months and if you're investing for 45 years or so, that's a short-lived experience. But in the middle of those 24 months, it can feel really awful. If you have a diversified portfolio, it doesn't hit as hard because usually
turns.zh: 表现差，我们就觉得明年也差。我觉得真正有帮助的是去看数据——我知道很多时候普通投资者并不愿意这么做——但熊市确实会发生。大多数熊市相当短暂，我会说不到 24 个月，如果你要投资大约 45 年，那只是很短的一段经历。可身处那 24 个月的中间，感觉真的很糟糕。如果你的组合是分散的，冲击就没那么猛烈，因为通常

turns.en: bonds and stocks move in somewhat opposite directions. In a severe downturn, they might start to move in the same direction. But I do think you can lessen the blow with diversity.
turns.zh: 债券和股票会大致朝相反方向走。在严重下跌中它们可能开始同向，但我确实认为分散能减轻冲击。

turns.en: I think if you have a long time horizon, it's not something you have to worry about. But I think it's very easy to say what the market is doing today is what it's going to do next month, next year, for the typical investor. Although we may intellectually know it's not true, but emotionally it feels like it's true. So you've talked about the psychology of spending, how it's really difficult to turn on spending after a lifetime of being a saver. Do you have any
turns.zh: 如果你的投资期限很长，这就不是你需要担心的事。但我觉得对普通投资者来说，太容易认定'今天市场的样子就是下个月、明年的样子'。虽然理智上我们知道不是真的，情绪上却觉得就是真的。我们刚才聊到花钱的心理——当了一辈子储蓄者之后，真的很难'打开'消费这档事。你有没有什么

turns.en: kind of best practices that you talk to people about in terms of getting warmed up to spend or giving themselves a little bit more permission to spend and really enjoy those early years of retirement, especially when their health is good and they might have pent up desires to travel or do things like that? How would you encourage them to get more comfortable with spending?
turns.zh: 最佳实践，跟人们讲怎么热身、怎么多给自己一点许可去花钱，真正享受退休头几年——尤其趁健康还不错、心里攒了很多想去旅行、想去做的事的时候？你会怎么鼓励他们更坦然地花钱？

turns.en: My favorite thing is so simple. It's just going to your brokerage house and turning on an automatic deposit into your checking account. So it shows up just like a paycheck. It's very similar to what happened during your working years. We know how to budget around it. We know how to spend around a paycheck. And I think automation is our friend. During our saving and accumulation years, automation is what gets you investing and it's what grows your wealth over time.
turns.zh: 我最喜欢的方法特别简单：去你的券商把自动转账打开，定期转到你的支票账户，让它像工资一样准时到账。这跟你工作年代的现金流几乎一样——我们本来就知道怎么围绕工资做预算、安排开支。我觉得自动化是我们的朋友。在储蓄积累的那些年里，是自动化让你坚持投资、让财富随时间增长的。

turns.en: Once we get to the decumulation, I think automation can help you spend. If that monthly money is coming in, it just shows up in your account. It doesn't feel like you're pulling out of your investments because it's just automatic. And I think that's probably the best thing you can do. I talked to so many retirees here just thinking, I can't touch this portfolio. I talked with one of my former high school teachers about two weeks ago. He and his wife have pensions,
turns.zh: 一旦进入消耗阶段，我觉得自动化同样能帮你花钱。这笔钱每月自动进账，就出现在你的账户里，你不会觉得是在从投资里'往外掏'，因为它只是自动发生。我觉得那大概是你能做的最好的事。我跟太多退休者聊过，他们就是想着'我不能碰这个组合'。大约两周前我跟我的一位高中老师聊过，他和太太有养老金，

turns.en: they have social security, and they're turning 73 this year. And they're like, we have to start taking our requirement on distributions. So we're going to start touching our investments. But to me, how crazy is that? You're almost a decade into retirement and you've never touched your investments. Go take another trip, help your kids out while you're alive and watch your legacy. I don't know. I just think, enjoy your money. It's just not meant to be
turns.zh: 有 Social Security，他们今年都 73 岁了。他们说：'我们得开始执行最低提取要求（RMD）了，我们得开始动用投资了。'但在我看来，这多疯狂啊？你已经退休快十年了，却从来没碰过你的投资。再去度一次假嘛，趁还活着帮帮你的孩子，看着你的传承（legacy）。我不知道——我就是想说，享受你的钱。钱不是只用来

turns.en: accumulated. One day we're going to die and you can't take it with you. So one of the reasons that people might be reluctant to spend is they're concerned about the potential need for long-term care and the costs associated with that. How do you think people can kind of mitigate that risk factor or think about planning for long-term care without being overly conservative? This one's a hard one because I think the media actively gives a
turns.zh: 攒的。人都有一死，你带不走它。所以，人们不敢花钱的原因之一，是担心潜在的长期护理需求和相关成本。你觉得人们怎样在不过度保守的前提下，缓释这个风险、做好长期护理的规划？这题很难，因为我觉得媒体呈现的图景是

turns.en: distorted picture. There's one of the stats that goes around constantly that 70% of Americans will need long-term care supports for services. And what gets lost in that stat is the supports or services part because we're not saying that 70% of Americans are going to need to be in a long-term care facility or a nursing facility. We're saying that they might need help after a surgery. They might need someone to help pick up their groceries or clean their home or help in some way with a
turns.zh: 扭曲的。有个数据一直在流传：70% 的美国人会需要长期护理的支持或服务。但这条数据里被丢掉的是'支持或服务'这几个字，因为这并不是说 70% 的人会需要住进长期护理机构或护理院，而是说：他们术后可能想有人搭把手，可能有人帮忙拎菜、打扫屋子，或者在

turns.en: daily activity, but it's not necessarily a stay in a long-term care facility. The number of people who truly end up in a long-term care facility is much smaller than that. I think it's in the neighborhood of maybe 10%. Don't quote me on that number, but it's much, much smaller than the 70%.
turns.zh: 日常活动的某些方面帮一下，但并不等于要住进长期护理机构。真正住进长期护理机构的人比那个少得多。我想大概在 10% 上下——这条数字别引用我——但远小于那 70%。

turns.en: And most people who end up in a long-term care facility, meeting stays around three years, nursing care facility, it's around one year. Now, it's not to say longer stays don't happen, but I don't think how the media presents it. I don't think it's conveyed in an accurate way.
turns.zh: 而且大多数住进长期护理机构的人，在机构里的平均停留大约三年；护理院的话，大约一年。我并不是说不存在更长的情况，但我不认同媒体呈现的那种方式，那种说法传达得并不准确。

turns.en: And if we look at a nursing care facility, if you end up in a Medicaid-approved nursing facility, if you go there when you're in a private pay situation and you totally deplete your assets, Medicaid will kick on and cover it. You don't have to move to a Medicaid facility truly, so you could stay where you are. So I do think there are more options than people realize.
turns.zh: 再看看护理院：如果你住进的是接受 Medicaid（联邦医疗补助）的护理院，你先以自费身份入住，等资产完全耗尽，Medicaid 就会接手支付。所以你其实不必真搬到只收 Medicaid 的机构，你可以就留在原地。所以我确实认为，人们手里的选项比意识到的要多。

turns.en: If you're looking at your portfolio in totality, if you are a homeowner, that would include the equity in your home. So you don't have to look at your portfolio and say, this fully has to carry long-term care. If I end up there, you could always tap home equity if that was an option that's available to you. So I think we have more resources than we give ourselves credit for at our disposal. And I don't think it's as big of a risk as media makes it out to be.
turns.zh: 如果你从整体看你的财务盘子，如果你是房主，那就该把房屋净值也算进去。所以你不必盯着自己的组合说'它必须独自扛起长期护理的全部费用'——万一我住进去了。你始终可以动用房屋净值，如果这条路对你可行。所以我觉得，我们拥有的资源比我们给自己打分的要多得多。我不觉得它像媒体渲染的那么可怕。

turns.en: The vast majority of people who retire will not end up in a long-term care facility or a nursing care facility or a memory care facility. Some people will, but the vast majority won't.
turns.zh: 绝大多数退休的人并不会住进长期护理机构、护理院或记忆照护机构。有人会遇到，但绝大多数不会。

turns.en: One dimension of the long-term care problem, it seems, is that a lot of care is getting provided by these unpaid family caregivers, often adult daughters. And I think that's a dimension that, yes, maybe there's no cost there, but there is a cost, right, to that person providing the care.
turns.zh: 长期护理问题似乎还有一个维度：大量的照护其实是由无偿的家庭照护者提供的，往往是成年女儿。我觉得这一层确实是——也许账面上没有支出，但对那位提供照护的人来说是有代价的，对吧？

turns.en: So can you talk about that? Because I do think that that is, if you're to ask some older adults, do you want your daughter to quit her job so that she can help you? Most people would say, no, I don't. So can you talk about that dimension of this issue?
turns.zh: 你能讲讲这一块吗？因为我确实觉得，如果去问一些年长者：'你希望你的女儿为了照顾你辞职吗？'大多数人会说'不，我不想'。所以，你能讲讲这个问题的这个维度吗？

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, there's a huge cost if you have to quit your job that's lost earnings, that's lost ability to save. So if a family member is doing this, there is absolutely a cost, even though you're not seeing it come out of the checkbook. I think this really comes down to family preferences. You know, if people go into retirement with a spouse, a lot of times it is the spouse who will end up caring for the spouse in declining health. And often that keeps that
turns.zh: 嗯，我是说，如果你不得不辞掉工作，那个代价是巨大的：那是收入的损失，是储蓄能力的丧失。所以如果有家庭成员在做这件事，代价是实打实存在的，只是你不会在账本上看出来。我觉得这件事最终取决于家庭的偏好。你知道，如果退休时身边有配偶，很多时候会是配偶在照护健康下滑的另一半，而这样做往往让那位配偶

turns.en: spouse out of a long-term care facility. If we speak about adult children, I don't know. I think it's a hard situation to navigate because I don't think people should be in a situation where they feel like they have to. Some family dynamics want to. I have a mom who is 75 years old. She has mobility issues, otherwise she's quite healthy. But I also think she lives a life where she's fairly isolated. And I've invited her to move in with me. My brother's invited her to move in
turns.zh: 免于住进长期护理机构。说到成年子女，我不知道——我觉得这是很难拿捏的处境。我不觉得谁应该被置于'不得不'的境地。有些家庭的氛围是他们愿意的。我妈 75 岁了，行动不太方便，但其他方面挺健康。不过我也觉得她的生活比较孤僻，我邀请她搬来跟我住，我哥也邀请她

turns.en: with him. And she says she's retiring this year, although I don't believe her because she's been saying that for 10 years. But I would be happy to have her here. And my family is very close, but she's also capable of taking care of herself. So I think that's a different dynamic. I wouldn't have to quit my job. I do think it's an incredible burden to ask your child to quit their job to take care of you. And whether or not people want to do that, that depends on their heritage,
turns.zh: 搬去他那儿。她说她今年要退休了，虽然我不信——她已经这么讲了十年了。但我真的很乐意让她来。我们家关系很亲，不过她也完全能自理。所以那是另一种动态，我并不需要辞掉我的工作。我确实觉得，要求你的孩子辞职来照顾你，是天大的负担。至于人们愿不愿意那么做，取决于他们的家族传统、

turns.en: their family situation, things like that. And maybe you want to find a way to compensate them. If you have an estate, maybe you give them a greater share when you pass on or something like that.
turns.zh: 家庭状况之类。也许你可以找一种方式来补偿他们。如果你有遗产，也许在你身后留给他们更大的份额，类似这样。

turns.en: If you can compensate, you should because there is a cost. And it seems like open communication is important, too, so that you don't have expectations that are sort of not clearly stated or understood by both parties.
turns.zh: 如果补偿得起，就应该补偿，因为那确实是有代价的。而且看起来，坦诚的沟通也很重要，这样双方才不会把一些没有明说、也没有被共同理解的期待挂在对方身上。

turns.en: Yes. And I would say I was very lucky that I grew up in a family where money was just talked about. I mean, we would talk about estates and inheritance. And we still do at the dinner table. And I know my sister-in-law sometimes looks at us and she's like, you guys are not normal because we will just talk about, hey, when you die, who is this going to? So if you can have that conversation openly without emotion, without judgment, I think that's helpful. One quite cute story I could give.
turns.zh: 对。我会说，我很幸运，我长大的家里钱就是可以摆在桌面上谈的。我们会聊遗产、聊继承，到今天在饭桌上照样聊。我嫂子有时会看着我们说：'你们家不正常。'因为我们就是会直接问：'你走了以后，这些东西归谁？'如果你能不带情绪、不带评判地这样聊开，我觉得很有帮助。还有个挺暖的小故事。

turns.en: My brother was in a financial position that was much better than me for many years. And he looked at me and he's like, oh, when dad passes away, you can have everything he has.
turns.zh: 我哥这些年的经济状况比我好很多。他有次看着我说：'哦，等爸爸走了，他那份你全拿去好了。'

turns.en: And then he was looking at buying a lake house. And he's like, oh, if this lake house goes through, I'm going to need half of dad's stuff. So those are the kind of conversations we'll have.
turns.zh: 然后他那阵在看一套湖边房子，他说：'哦，要是这套房买成了，我可能就需要我爸那边的一半了。'我们家就是这样聊的。

turns.en: You also write a lot about social security planning and maximizing social security. Do you have any favorite tools that people can use to figure out when they should be starting their benefits? I don't know if I have any tools to recommend. It's probably a situation where it's really good to talk with an advisor. I have a general expression that I use that is if you can afford to delay, I think it's a better retirement. You can increase your income floor,
turns.zh: 你也写了很多关于 Social Security 领取规划和最大化的内容。你有没有什么称手的工具，能帮人们判断什么时候该开始领取？我不好说我有什么工具可以推荐，这可能真的是'最好跟顾问好好聊聊'的情况。我有一句常挂在嘴边的话：如果你拖得起，我会说晚一点领是更好的退休——你可以抬高你的收入底线（income floor），

turns.en: but not everyone has the resources to retire. Maybe you're in a family that has a lower life expectancy, maybe you have health issues, maybe you're forced out of the workforce earlier than you planned. So there's a lot of situations where it can make sense to claim early.
turns.zh: 但不是人人都有那个资源。也许你的家族预期寿命偏短，也许你有健康问题，也许你被迫比计划更早离开职场。所以有很多情形下，早点申领是说得通的。

turns.en: But my general stance is if you can afford to delay, whether that's working longer, you have the assets to cover that gap, it makes a lot of sense because then it takes pressure off your portfolio for the remainder of your life. If people are married, I generally see that staggered claiming leads to higher lifetime benefits and a little bit more security, less pressure off the portfolio. So again, individual situations. So Erin, you mentioned that you
turns.zh: 但我的总体立场是：如果你拖得起——不管是多工作几年，还是有资产能补上这段空缺——那就很划算，因为它给你余生的投资组合减压。如果已婚，我一般认为错峰领取（staggered claiming）会带来更高的终身福利、多一点安全感、组合的压力也更小。所以还是那句话，看个人情况。Erin，你之前提到过，

turns.en: like to push back on concerns about the future of social security. There are certainly a lot of doomsayers out there. Can you talk about why you think that people who are, say, over 50 should feel some comfort that their promised benefits will be there for them when they go to claim?
turns.zh: 你会反驳那些对 Social Security 未来的担忧。外面确实一大堆唱衰的人。你能讲讲，为什么你觉得比如说 50 岁以上的人，可以比较安心地相信：等到他们去申领的那天，承诺的福利会在那里等着他们？

turns.en: I mean, point blank, people over 50 vote and those in Congress know it. So if they upset that population, it's not going to be well for them. They're going to lose their job.
turns.zh: 我是说，打开天窗说亮话：50 岁以上的人会投票，国会那帮人心里门儿清。他们要是把这批人得罪狠了，日子就不好过——他们会丢了位子。

turns.en: I think Congress has a huge motivation to act. I do think social security will experience reform and will see changes. I don't necessarily know what those changes would be, whether it's reducing costs of living adjustments going forward, increasing the wage cap. I mean, there might be the potential that they try to borrow in order to fund the trust fund, which we've never done before. They would have
turns.zh: 我觉得国会有极强的动机去行动。我确实认为 Social Security 会经历改革、会有变化。我说不准具体会改什么——也许是压低未来的生活成本调整（COLA），也许是提高应税工资上限。我的意思是，甚至有可能他们试图借钱来给信托基金注资，这种事我们以前从没做过。他们得

turns.en: to rewrite the laws, but there's going to be a way in which they keep social security going forward. And I think people over 50 don't have to worry about changes to their benefits. I think people in my generation, 30s, I think benefits will change, but benefits will be there. The narrative is often that social security is going bankrupt, and that's not true. There are current workers today who are paying into the system, and that pays out to the current retirees today. So
turns.zh: 重写法律，但总会有一条路让 Social Security 走下去。我觉得 50 岁以上的人不必担心自己的福利被改动。我这一代人，30 多岁的，我觉得福利会变，但福利不会没有。外面的叙事往往是'Social Security 要破产了'，那不是事实。今天仍在职的人在往这个体系里缴钱，这些钱付给了今天的退休者。所以

turns.en: it would still be able to pay out what's coming in, which currently is about 77% of what the payouts would be, but I don't think benefits would be cut for near term or current retirees.
turns.zh: 体系靠流入的资金仍然能付出一部分，目前大概是应付额的 77%。但我不觉得近期退休者或当前退休者的福利会被削减。

turns.en: So if you're a younger person trying to plan for retirement, would you sort of look at your future social security benefits and maybe give those a haircut to account for potential reductions in future benefits, or how would you handle those potential changes?
turns.zh: 那如果你是一位正在规划退休的年轻人，你会不会对未来的 Social Security 福利打个折扣，来给可能的削减留出缓冲？你会怎么处理这些潜在变化？

turns.en: Generally, if I'm talking to somebody who's in their 20s, 30s, or even their early 40s, I don't even want them considering social security at that point, not that I don't think it's going to be there. I think it will be, but I want you saving and investing in a way where you're not relying on it because I'd rather you get to retirement and say, oh, I have more than enough, or I can potentially retire early, or I can take extra vacations that I didn't think I was going to.
turns.zh: 总体上，如果我跟二十多岁、三十岁甚至四十出头的人聊，我压根不想让他们现在就把 Social Security 算进盘算——不是说我觉得它不会在。我觉得它会在，但我希望你储蓄和投资的方式是不依赖它的，因为我宁愿你在退休时发现'哦，我的钱比需要的多'、'我或许可以提前退休'、'我可以多度几个原本没指望的假'。

turns.en: It's a better position to get to retirement and have more money rather than less. I think once you get to late 40s and 50s, and especially in your 60s, I mean, you're already at social security age, I would look at what those benefits are. I'd build my budget, figure out what my gap is between what social security is and how much I want to spend. But prior to 45 or something, save and invest as if you're kind of blind to what those social security benefits would be.
turns.zh: 带着多出来的钱进入退休，总好过带着不够的钱。到了 40 多岁后段、50 多岁，尤其到了 60 多岁——反正你已经到 Social Security 领取年龄了——这时候我会去看你的福利具体有多少，搭好预算，算出 Social Security 和你想花的钱之间的缺口。但在那之前，大概 45 岁以前，你就当自己看不见那些 Social Security 福利，只管储蓄、只管投资。

turns.en: You often talk about social security pitfalls or mistakes that people can make. What are the big ones that people should be aware of? I think one of the biggest is one we already touched on, thinking that the trust fund is going to be totally depleted, meaning that there wouldn't be benefits for you, or that your benefits would be cut. I hear so many people right now saying, claim as early as you can,
turns.zh: 你也常讲 Social Security 的坑、人们容易犯的错误。大家最该警惕的大错误有哪些？我觉得最大的一个我们其实已经碰到了——以为信托基金会被彻底掏空，也就是说你压根领不到福利，或者你的福利会被砍。我现在听到太多人说：'能多早领就多早领，

turns.en: so you can get something while it's there. I just think that that's a fearful mentality, and the more we operate out of fear, the worst decisions we tend to make. I think if I look back over the course of my life, I have not made great decisions if I made them out of fear.
turns.zh: 趁东西还在先捞一笔。'我只觉得，那是恐惧驱动的心态。我们越是出于恐惧行事，做的决定往往越差。回看我这辈子，凡是因为恐惧做出来的决定，都不是好决定。

turns.en: I would bring it back to what my budget looks like, what my portfolio looks like, and really how much security do I need. There's great value in having a reliable income stream that is inflation adjusted for the remainder of your life. Build around what you truly need in your plan, in your budget, and look at what you might need for the next couple of decades, and truly look at what size portfolio you have, and what kind of gap you can fill,
turns.zh: 我会把话题拉回到：我的预算长什么样？我的组合长什么样？我到底需要多少安全感？一条贯穿余生、跟着通胀调整的可靠收入流，价值巨大。围绕你计划里、预算里真正需要的东西去搭建，想想未来二三十年可能需要什么，认真掂量你手上的组合有多大、能填上多少空缺，

turns.en: and make your decision based on that. If you're married, factor in that one of you is going to pass away first. It makes a lot of sense in many cases to have the higher earning spouse delay because whoever passes away, they get to keep the higher earners benefit, and that can provide a lot of security to the surviving spouse.
turns.zh: 再基于这些做决定。如果已婚，要算上你们之中必然有一个人会先走。很多情况下，让收入更高的那一方延后领取非常合理，因为无论谁先去世，健在的那位都能保留较高那份福利——这能给在世配偶极大的安全感。

turns.en: What's your take on annuities as a component of retirement planning? There's a lot of strong opinions on both sides. There are retirement experts and academics who say annuity should be much more broadly used, but other people are very anti-annuity. Do you have a take on that?
turns.zh: 你怎么看年金（annuities）作为退休规划的一个组成部分？两边都有很强的观点。有退休领域的专家和学者认为年金应该被更广泛地使用，也有人非常反年金。你有立场吗？

turns.en: And what type of annuity do you think works best for most retirees? A lot of times, I'll say that annuities are like a four-letter word in retirement because, my gosh, if you talk about an annuity, oh, do you get pushed back? I'm kind of neutral on them.
turns.zh: 你觉得哪类年金对多数退休者最合适？很多时候我会说：年金在退休话题里简直像个'四字脏话'。天哪，你一谈年金，就会被怼回来。我对年金算是中立。

turns.en: I would say when I started my financial career, I was pretty anti-annuity because I'm a bogelhead, and I'm an index investor, and I want to avoid all fees at all possible costs.
turns.zh: 我可以说，我刚入行的时候相当反年金，因为我是个 Boglehead（指数投资信徒）、我是指数投资者，我想不惜一切代价避开所有费用。

turns.en: As I've gotten older and as I do retirement research and talk to a lot of retirees, I think there is definitely a place for annuities. I don't think they're right for everyone. I think they're a tool that can be implemented, especially for those retirees who are scared to spend.
turns.zh: 随着我年纪增长、做退休研究、跟大量退休者交流之后，我觉得年金绝对有一席之地。我不觉得它适合所有人，但它是一种可以用起来的工具，尤其对那些不敢花钱的退休者。

turns.en: If you're truly scared to spend from your portfolio, I think it's a great way to mimic an income. And so if you're willing to annuitize a portion of your portfolio, maybe it's 25, 30%, certainly not all of it, I think it can make a lot of sense if it provides the sense of safety.
turns.zh: 如果你真的不敢从自己的组合里往外花钱，我觉得它是'模拟一份收入'的好方法。所以如果你愿意把组合的一部分年金化——也许 25%、30%，肯定不是全部——如果它能带来安全感，我觉得就很说得通。

turns.en: And maybe at that point, you're willing to invest the remainder of your portfolio in a slightly more aggressive fashion so you could capture higher returns or potentially capture higher returns over the course of your retirement suite, still have a legacy to leave if that was something you're interested in. If I'm talking about annuities that I like, I would probably say immediate annuities or deferred income annuities. They have
turns.zh: 而且到那时候，你也许反而愿意把剩下的组合投得稍微进取一点，从而在你的退休期间捕获更高的收益——或者说有机会捕获更高的回报——同时还能留下一笔传承，如果你在乎这个的话。如果说我认可的年金，我大概会挑即时年金（immediate annuity）或延期起付年金（deferred income annuity）。它们的

turns.en: lesser fees and lesser complexity. And I think the more complex the product, generally the more fees associated with it. And I just think if you can't explain it clearly, if you don't know exactly where the fees are, I don't trust the product. So it has to be able to be explained simply. And I think those are the two most transparent annuities.
turns.zh: 费用更低、复杂度也更低。我觉得产品越复杂，通常绑定的费用就越多。我就是觉得，如果你没法把产品讲清楚、搞不明白费用到底藏在哪里，我就不信这个产品。它必须能被简单地解释。我认为这两种就是最透明的年金。

turns.en: It seems like one of the main things annuities have going for them is just, as you said, that simple paycheck that gets deposited in my account.
turns.zh: 看起来，年金最大的一个优点，正是你说的那样——就像那份每个月准时打进我账户的简单工资。

turns.en: You have talked about how your dad fell prey to a Ponzi scheme he experienced dementia later in life. Can you talk about what you took away from that experience?
turns.zh: 你讲过你父亲中了庞氏骗局（Ponzi scheme）的圈套，晚年又患上失智症（dementia）。你能讲讲那段经历让你学到了什么吗？

turns.en: My dad has made every financial mistake in the book. So I learned a lot from him over the years. He used to have this saying that you can always make more money. So it didn't really matter how you invested it or how you spent it. Or he also had the philosophy that he wanted to die a million dollars in debt. So he didn't care if he took on debt either.
turns.zh: 我爸爸基本上把理财教科书里的错误全犯了一遍。所以这些年我从他身上学到了很多。他以前有句话，说'钱嘛，永远能再赚'，所以你投得怎么样、花得怎么样都无所谓。他还有一种哲学，说他想'背着一百万美元的债死去'，所以他连欠债也不在乎。

turns.en: I think from him, I learned a great work ethic. I learned to earn money. Oh, man, I don't know. I think from him, I learned that maybe it's okay to sometimes call in a professional to manage your finances. If he had had an advisor, he wouldn't have gone through what he did. He wouldn't have invested in a Ponzi scheme. And he wouldn't have invested in all these IPOs. We wouldn't have had these huge conversions to gold. We wouldn't have had short
turns.zh: 从他身上，我想我学到了极强的工作伦理，学会了怎么挣钱。天哪，我不知道——从他身上我也学到：有时候请个专业的人来帮你管钱也未尝不可。如果他有一位顾问，他就不会经历他所经历的那些。他不会投进庞氏骗局，也不会去追那一大堆 IPO，我们也不会看到那么大规模的

turns.en: sales on homes. Just every mistake in the book, I can't even tell you. But he was probably somebody who needed a professional in his corner because he was quite impulsive as his memory started declining. He was married at the time. It was a second marriage he got taken advantage of.
turns.zh: 换成黄金的操作，也不会有卖房做空这种事。真的是书里写的错误全犯完了，我说都说不完。但他可能恰恰是那种身边需要一位专业人士把关的人，因为他在记忆力开始下滑时非常冲动。当时他已经再婚，那是他的第二段婚姻——他被人占了便宜。

turns.en: It was just not a good situation. I mean, in total, my brother and I figured out he probably lost a million and a half on crummy investments throughout the course of his life.
turns.zh: 那真的不是一个好的处境。我是说，总共算下来，我和我哥推测，他这一辈子因为糟糕的投资大概亏掉了约 150 万美元（$1.5 million）。

turns.en: That's a big number, for sure. So if people are thinking about cognitive decline, are there best practices that older adults and their advisors can use to protect their finances as they get older? I think this one's really hard. There were signs that my dad had memory issues that I didn't see in the moment, but I recognized them in hindsight. My last lunch that I had with him before he was admitted to a memory care facility, it was probably seven or eight months prior to
turns.zh: 那当然是个大数字。那么，如果人们考虑到认知衰退这件事，年长者和他们的顾问有什么最佳实践，可以在他们老去的过程中保护自己的财务？我觉得这件事真的很难。我爸爸其实早就有记忆力出问题的迹象，只是当时我没看出来，事后回想才认得出来。他被送进记忆照护机构之前，我跟他吃的最后一顿午饭，大概是在那之前

turns.en: that happening. And I remember at the start of lunch, he asked me, hey, how are things going? Because I didn't live in the area he lived and I didn't visit him that often. And we had that conversation of what was going on in my life and what was new. And then we got about 15 minutes in the conversation and he's like, oh, hey, how's it going? And I just thought it was weird that he brought it up again. And I didn't really catch it. So I think it's subtle. And I think you have
turns.zh: 七八个月。我记得刚坐下他就问我：'最近怎么样啊？'因为我不在他住的地方生活，也不常去看他。于是我们聊了聊我的生活、有什么新鲜事。大概聊到 15 分钟，他又来一句：'哦，最近怎么样？'我当时只觉得奇怪——他怎么又问了一遍。可我也没真的当回事。所以我觉得，信号是很微妙的，你非得

turns.en: to really pay attention and be around this person on a more regular basis. So if someone's getting older, I would say it's a really good idea to loop in somebody who knows them and has their best interests, you know, whether that is an adult child, whether that's a spouse, have them come to meetings with a financial advisor. I'm a huge fan of the DIY approach, keeping costs low. I love that during the investing years because I want people to build as much wealth as they can.
turns.zh: 非常留心，而且要经常跟这个人待在一起才行。所以，如果有人在变老，我会说，非常值得把一位既了解他、又真心为他好的人拉进这个局——不管是一位成年子女，还是配偶——让他们一起来见理财顾问。我是 DIY 路线的铁杆粉丝，我喜欢低成本。我喜欢在积累的那些年里用 DIY，因为我想让人们尽可能把财富做大。

turns.en: But I also have acknowledged that when you get to the later stages of life, most of us will experience some level of cognitive decline. I mean, certainly most people are not going to get dementia or Alzheimer's, but some level of decline. And we're just not as sharp as we were in our 40s and 50s. So I think it's a good idea to loop someone in who can kind of be this neutral party who can say, well, maybe this isn't the great idea. Maybe we should reevaluate this.
turns.zh: 但我同时也不得不承认，到了人生后半段，我们大多数人都会经历某种程度的认知下降。当然，绝大多数人并不会得失智症或阿尔茨海默病，但总会有一些下滑，我们不会还像 40 岁、50 岁时那样敏锐。所以我觉得，引入一个能充当'中立第三方'的人是好主意，那个人可以说：'嗯，这个主意也许没那么好，我们是不是该重新评估一下？'

turns.en: Yeah, I like that you often talk about the value of financial advice, especially as people move into their retirement years. Do you have any sort of talking points in terms of finding someone who's trustworthy? What's on your shortlist of criteria that people should have when seeking financial advice?
turns.zh: 对，我很欣赏你常说的那一点——理财建议的价值，尤其当人们走进退休的那几年。关于怎么找到一个信得过的人，你有没有一些可以拿去用的挑选要点？在你心里的'标准短名单'上，人们在寻求理财建议时应该看什么？

turns.en: I always start with looking for someone who's NAPA certified. I think I notice a big distinction between advisors who are and aren't. I really like someone who is personable and takes, you should have a handful of meetings with this person. It shouldn't be a one-off. They shouldn't know your goals. They should know your budget. They should know your story of why you're retiring, how you got where you got, what kind of legacy you want to leave, what your goals are in
turns.zh: 我总是先看这个人有没有 NAPFA 认证。我能明显感觉到，有认证和没认证的顾问之间差别很大。我很看重亲和力，而且你应该跟这个人见上好几轮，不该是一锤子买卖。他们应该了解你的目标，了解你的预算，了解你的故事——你为什么退休、怎么走到今天的、你想留下什么样的传承、你在退休里的

turns.en: retirement. I just think it's so complex that you can't handle it in one meeting. I think you also want somebody who seems to care about you and care about your money in the same way you do.
turns.zh: 目标是什么。我觉得这件事太复杂了，一次会面根本搞定不了。我还觉得，你要找一个看起来真的在乎你、也在乎你的钱、像你一样在意的人。

turns.en: Obviously no one's going to care about your money more than you, but you should not be seen as a walking paycheck for them. Sometimes you'll get that vibe from an investor and I wouldn't stick with them. You want somebody who sees you as a person and wants to protect you as a person.
turns.zh: 当然没人会比你更在乎你的钱，但你绝不能觉得自己在那人眼里只是'一张会走路的薪水支票'。有时候你跟某个顾问打交道就有那种感觉，换我我就不会继续跟他做。你要找的是那种把你当人看、愿意保护你的人。

turns.en: I guess I would also add someone who's not trying to sell you commission-based products, because I think there's a big disincentive there. Right. You recently took a position as lead financial educator at Root Financial.
turns.zh: 我想我还要补一句：找不向你推销佣金型产品的人，因为那里面的激励错位太大了。对。你最近出任了 Root Financial 的首席金融教育官（lead financial educator）。

turns.en: How did you decide to align with Root and how will that affect the work you do at Aaron Talks Money, if at all? It doesn't really affect it. I've tried to be very clear with my audience about that. Again, I am a DIY investor. I want people to understand their money. I want them to take the reins on their money and if they can, throughout the entirety of their life, manage their finances on their own, great. I love that approach and I hope that I can do that for my entire
turns.zh: 你是怎么决定与 Root 牵手的？这会如何影响你在 Erin Talks Money 上做的工作，如果有的话？其实没什么影响。我努力跟观众讲清楚：我依然是 DIY 投资者。我想让人们看懂自己的钱，我想让他们握紧自己钱的缰绳——如果他们在整个一生都能自己管理自己的财务，那太好了。我热爱这条路，我希望我一辈子都能这么走下去。

turns.en: life. I can't guarantee I will be in my 70s or 80s, but that's my belief that I would like to. And I think there are many people who are very skilled. They have great financial literacy and they're capable of that, but there are many people who want the guidance of an investor.
turns.zh: 我不敢保证到了 70、80 岁的我还是这样，但那是我此刻的信念。我觉得这世上有很多很有本事的人，他们金融素养很好，完全有能力自己搞定。但也有很多人的确想要一位顾问来指点。

turns.en: There are many people who don't want to manage the day-to-day activities of their money and handle Roth conversions and Medicaid decisions and minimizing their taxes in retirement, and not everyone has the same level of financial literacy. So, if you get an advisor who can save you tens of thousands of dollars in taxes or in whatever method they're planning, if they can help you sell a business, if they can help you reduce your income so that you're able to build up a larger
turns.zh: 有很多人不想每天打理钱的具体事务——不想处理 Roth 转换（Roth conversions），不想做 Medicaid 决策，不想在退休期间把税降到最低——并不是每个人金融素养都在同一水位。所以，如果你找到一位顾问，能帮你省下几万美元的税金，或者以他们的规划方式帮你省下别的——如果他们能帮你卖掉一家企业、帮你压低应税收入，好让你攒下更大的

turns.en: retirement, reduce your taxable income, I should say, I think they can be well worth their weight in gold. But Erin talks money will not change. I'm focused on education and helping people with their financial literacy. But I would also say on a daily basis, I have people reaching out to me through email, through LinkedIn, through the YouTube channel, and they are looking for an advisor. And I would feel so bad when people would email me and say, hey, will you manage my money?
turns.zh: 退休储备——我是说压低应税收入——我觉得他们真的值千金。但 Erin Talks Money 不会变。我依然聚焦在教育、在提升大家的金融素养上。但我也想说的是，几乎每天都有人通过邮件、通过 LinkedIn、通过 YouTube 频道来找我，他们在找顾问。以前有人给我发邮件问：'你帮我管钱吗？'

turns.en: Or can you point me to an advisor? And I didn't have anyone to point them to. I already work 50 hours a week. I'm not taking on another job. I have a toddler, so I'm busy. So I vetted root for probably eight to nine months before I agreed to the position. I talked to clients there. I talked to James, who's the owner. I talked to their lead team. I talked to advisors. I talked to everyone imaginable. And this is a good company. And I feel good about recommending people there.
turns.zh: '或者你能给我指一位顾问吗？'那时候我真的很难受，因为我没有人可以推荐给他们。我每周已经工作 50 小时了，我不会再接一份工作。我还有个刚会走路的小娃，我很忙。所以在答应这个职位之前，我考察了 Root 大概八到九个月。我跟他们的客户聊过，跟老板 James 聊过，跟他们的核心团队聊过，跟顾问聊过，我能想到的所有人都聊了一遍。这是一家好公司。把人推荐去那里，我心里是踏实的。

turns.en: So for the people who are looking for an advisor, it's a wonderful place to go. For the people who want to DIY it, keep DIYing it. So Amy and I have both written about our own money foibles, or the weird things that we do with our own money. Do you have anything that you do that you would put in that category of do as I say, not as I do, that here's a decision that I'm making that doesn't necessarily dovetail with the conventional wisdom about how to manage money?
turns.zh: 所以，对那些正在找顾问的人，那里是非常好的去处。对那些想继续 DIY 的人，请继续 DIY。Amy 和我都写过自己在钱上的一些小毛病——就是我们自己在自己的钱上做的怪事。你自己有没有什么事，会归到'照我说的做、别照我做的做'那一类？也就是说，你自己在做的、不一定跟主流理财智慧吻合的决定？

turns.en: Yeah, I would say a couple of them. Some I've been shielded from, but I tried to make the mistakes. In my 20s, I was kind of like a little bit of a martyr. I would just save every single penny possible. Again, my goal was fire. I also had a very driven scarcity mindset. I became quite ill when I was 18 years old. I had a brain tumor. I was paralyzed on the right side of my body, and I lost my ability to work, my ability to earn an income. I was so fearful that that would
turns.zh: 嗯，我想有好几个。有些我算是被挡在了外面，但我自己去试过那些错。二十多岁的时候，我有点像个小苦行僧，能省的一分我都省。我当时的目标就是 FIRE，我骨子里还有非常强烈的稀缺心态。我 18 岁的时候生过一场大病——我长了脑瘤，右边身体瘫痪了，我失去了工作能力、失去了收入的能力。我特别害怕那种事

turns.en: happen again, or that there would be another health crisis. I felt like I had to save what I could when I could, and I would just work. I would work two or three jobs, and I just saved every penny of income. I can look back on that and say, I missed a lot of years of friendships and activities, and being able to enjoy life a little bit more because I was so focused on saving, and I was doing it out of fear. I look at people who enjoyed their 20s a little bit more, and I'm
turns.zh: 再次发生，或者又来一场健康危机。我觉得我必须趁能挣的时候能存就存。我就一直工作，打两三份工，把每一分收入都存下来。现在回头看，我可以说：我错过了很多年的友情、活动，本来可以稍微享受一下人生，因为我太专注于存钱了，而且那是出于恐惧。看着别人在二十几岁里稍微享受得多一点，我会有

turns.en: a little bit envious of that. As I got into my 30s, I kind of had to learn to spend because I had never really done it before, and it was kind of nice going from the generic catch up to Heinz catch up or taking a vacation. I was like, oh, this is what life is supposed to feel like.
turns.zh: 一点点羡慕。到了三十多岁，我不得不学着花钱，因为我从来没真的花过。从那种普通的'补课式存钱'升级成讲究一点的'补课'、或者说去度个假，那种感觉其实挺好，我心里说：'哦，原来生活本该是这个味道。'

turns.en: I'm still a budget queen. A lot of times I say I'm a baller on a budget, but I would say spend a little bit more because you shouldn't have any throwaway years. All years of your life should be valuable. This year, I almost made a big financial mistake.
turns.zh: 我现在仍然是预算女王。我常自嘲是'预算内的阔太'，但我会说，多花一点点吧，因为你不该有任何'浪费掉的年份'，人生的每一年都该有价值。今年，我差点犯一个大错。

turns.en: I was aware I was doing it, but it didn't work out. I bought a home last year, and I love my home. It's okay. It's great, but I found another home across town that was on this cul-de-sac, and it was surrounded with young moms and dads and young kids, and there was a park right there, and it was so great. I'm like, oh, I want my kid to grow up here. I almost bought a new house within nine months of buying another, and I kind of looked at it as, hey, if I do this,
turns.zh: 我当时其实知道自己在干什么，只是最后没成。我去年买了房，我很爱我的房子，挺好的，真的挺好。但我在城的另一头看到一套房子，在一个死胡同社区（cul-de-sac）里，周围全是年轻爸妈和小孩，旁边就有一个公园，太好了。我心里就想：我想让我的孩子在这里长大。我在买了另一套才九个月之内又想买一套，我当时的心态是：'如果我这么做，

turns.en: my dad's words, I can just make more money, and I know I would lose money on the deal, but it doesn't matter because quality of life. Ultimately, that deal didn't work out, but I would have happily taken the stupid tax on that one, and then long-term, I thought it would have been a better quality of life. Sometimes you have to be willing to go after what's more important in life decisions than just the financial decisions because
turns.zh: 用我爸的话说——钱还能再赚。'我知道这笔买卖我会亏钱，但那没关系，因为生活质量。最后这笔没谈成。但我本来是乐意交这笔'愚蠢税'（stupid tax）的，从长远看，我觉得那会换来更好的生活质量。有时候，你必须愿意去追人生中比'纯财务上划算'更重要的东西，

turns.en: you have to find the greatest happiness in life. One question we like to put to our guests is where they go for financial insights, whether it's a podcast, a columnist, blogger, an author. I like Jason Fickner. Those are both
turns.zh: 因为人得找到此生最大的幸福。我们常问嘉宾的一个问题是：你从哪里获取财务洞见——播客、专栏作者、博主、作者？你会提名谁是你的心头好？我想我报几个名字吧。我喜欢 Michael Kitces 的研究，我喜欢 Wade Pfau，我喜欢 Andrew Biggs，我觉得他特别公允、特别冷静。我喜欢 Jason Fichtner。后面这两位

turns.en: former deputy commissioners of Social Security. David Blanchett, I know he's part of the Morningstar team, or I think he is. Is he? He was, no longer. He's a credential now.
turns.zh: 都曾担任 Social Security 署的副专员。还有 David Blanchett，我知道他是 Morningstar 团队的人——或者说我想他是？他现在还在吗？他曾经是，现在不了。他现在算是独立顾问了。

turns.en: I think he does wonderful research. Christine Benz here on this podcast. I followed your work forever. I also just read every single book that comes out on finance and retirement. If there's a new release this month, I've probably read it. Oddly enough, being that my platform is YouTube, I don't really watch financial content that much. I might catch one video a week or one video every two weeks, but I spend so much time writing my own scripts and filming them that
turns.zh: 我觉得他的研究做得非常棒。还有 Christine Benz，就在这档播客上——我一直拜读你的作品。另外基本上每一本新出的金融和退休书我都会读，这个月要是有新书，我大概率读完了。说来也怪，虽然我自己的平台就是 YouTube，我倒不太看别人的金融内容。我一礼拜也许就看一条视频，或者两礼拜一条，但我花了太多时间写自己的脚本、拍自己的视频，

turns.en: I don't want to be on YouTube longer than that. I would say it's books and it's blogs and it's podcasts. A lot of research articles, too. Well, Erin, this has been such a treat to chat with you today. Congratulations on your success. Your YouTube channel is a juggernaut. It's amazing.
turns.zh: 所以我不想再在 YouTube 上多待了。我会说，我的信息来自书、博客、播客，还有大量的研究文章。Erin，今天跟你聊真的是大大的享受。祝贺你取得的成功，你的 YouTube 频道就是一台势不可挡的机器，太厉害了。

turns.en: Thank you so much for being here. Thank you for having me. It's really a pleasure and honor. Thanks so much, Erin. We really enjoyed talking with you.
turns.zh: 真的太谢谢你们了。谢谢邀请，这是我的荣幸，也非常开心。太谢谢你了，Erin，我们聊得特别尽兴。
